title: Adjectives and adverbs
tagline: A big red bag, a bored student, a boring film: describing people, things and actions.
why: Adjectives and adverbs make your English colourful: instead of 'a bag', you can say 'a big red bag'; instead of 'ran', you can say 'ran quickly'. The exam tests small but important choices — bored or boring, good or well — in Reading Part 5 and in your own writing and speaking.

hook.text: In the school magazine office, Liam looks at photos. "This one is boring," he says. "No, it's lovely! Look at that big green field," says Nadia. "And everyone looks so excited!"
hook.ask: Can you find the words that describe things? Two of them look similar — boring and excited — but they work in different ways. Can you guess why?

diagrams.title: Where does the adjective go?

sentences.note: adjective after be — no noun needed

diagrams.caption: An adjective can sit right before a noun, or after be / look / feel / taste with no noun at all.

diagrams.title: Making adverbs with -ly

rules.rule: Ends in -y: y becomes i + ly

diagrams.caption: Fast and hard look like adjectives and adverbs at the same time — don't add -ly to them.

rows.label: Describes
cells: the thing that causes the feeling

use.point: Adjectives before the noun and after be/look/feel

examples.note: adjective after taste, look or feel — no -ly here

use.point: Two adjectives together: the order matters

examples.text: We saw a small brown dog in the park.

use.point: -ed or -ing: who feels it, what causes it

examples.note: bored = how I feel, boring = what it's like
same pattern: person feels it, thing causes it

examples.text: Miss Vega was tired after a tiring day.
examples.note: the day is tiring, so Miss Vega is tired

use.point: Adverbs and how much: manner and intensifiers

examples.text: Liam ran quickly to catch the bus.
This bag is too heavy for me to carry.
examples.note: too + adjective = more than you want

examples.text: I'm not tall enough to reach the shelf.
The film wasn't very exciting, but it was quite good.
examples.note: very/really/quite show how strong the adjective is

watch_out.why: Size comes before colour in English word order.
Use -ed for how you feel, not -ing.
Well is the adverb for good, not good itself.

watch_out.wrong: It's enough big for two people.
watch_out.why: Enough goes after the adjective, not before.
Too goes before the adjective, not after.

l1.why: Spanish can put the colour first; English always puts size before colour.
Spanish bien looks like good, but the adverb in English is well.
Boring describes the thing that causes boredom, not the person who feels it.

l1.wrong: It's very expensive for me to buy.
l1.right: It's too expensive for me to buy.
l1.why: Demasiado means more than you want — that's too, not very.

remember.trick: Big before red. -ed is you, -ing is the thing!
remember.tip: Size comes before colour, and if YOU feel it use -ed; if THE THING causes it, use -ing.

dialogue.title: Choosing a photo for the yearbook
dialogue.context: Sofia, Liam and Nadia look through photos for the school yearbook while Miss Vega listens.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Look at this one! It's a lovely old photo of the football team.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I don't like it. The colours are boring.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: This one is better — a big green field and everyone is smiling.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good choice. Does anyone look bored or tired in that photo? No — everyone looks excited!

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Liam looks really happy in this photo.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: That's because we won easily! It wasn't a difficult match.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: This photo is too dark, though. Can we choose a brighter one?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes, that one's bright enough for the front page.

can_do: I can put two adjectives in the right order, like a big red bag.
I can tell the difference between bored and boring.
I can use -ly adverbs and words like well, too and enough to describe actions.
summary: Put adjectives in the right order: size before colour, like a big red bag.
Use -ed for how you feel and -ing for what causes the feeling: I'm bored, the film is boring.
Most adverbs add -ly to the adjective, but good → well, and fast/hard don't change.
Too means more than you want; enough comes after the adjective: too heavy, tall enough.
